items.title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
items.content:
I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.

Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP —hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis , which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4 —a lower bound (!!) , matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log 2 7) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.

Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that !

But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N) 1/2+o(1) . The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log 0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!) . All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered , rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.

To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE —that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.

It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next. It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.

I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.

For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden. Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between. Just please don’t deny what’s happening. Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean…

items.title: GTA 6 Publisher Furious as Reverse Engineers Get It Running on PC: It's happening whether Rockstar Games likes it or not.
items.content:
As pretty much everybody expected, the sixth installment of the hit video game series Grand Theft Auto is off to a roaring start.

Take-Two Interactive, the company that owns GTA 6 developer Rockstar Games, proudly announced last week that retail sales had reached a record $3.79 billion in a single day, making it the biggest entertainment — not just gaming — launch in history.

However, thanks to the company’s exclusivity agreements with Microsoft and Sony, PC gamers are currently completely excluded from playing the game.

While those players would conventionally stew in silence, awaiting a PC port that could take months if not years to hit the market, the advent of AI coding tools has upended that status quo. Now, GTA 6 has become their number one target . Take-Two has already tried to scrub several ports of the massively popular game from the internet, as IGN reports , convincing GitHub to delete a network of over 3,000 code repositories via a DMCA takedown notice.

But it’s a game of cat and mouse as more projects come online on a daily basis, many of which are making major strides toward turning a PC version of GTA 6 into a playable experience.

Screenshots and short clips being shared widely on social media show the game running on PCs. However, the ports appear to be running at extremely low frame rates for the time being, suggesting modders have plenty of optimizing left to do. But considering we’re less than a single week into the game’s release, it’s an astonishing amount of progress nonetheless.

That means what could soon turn into the best-selling video game of all time may become extremely easy to pirate and play on the device of the gamer’s choosing. On one hand, it’s a for the considerable proportion of gamers who’ve been done dirty by console exclusive experiences. On the other, it’s a development that could lead to even more locked down games as publishers desperately try to clamp down on the practice.

items.title: 1Password Security Incident
items.content:
On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:

Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.

When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning . During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.

1Password does not store your account password or secret key

Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.

Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.

Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.

Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.

Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.

1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.

Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.

If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.

You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Entering the Geminispace
items.content:
On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread . I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that.

However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ . The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post.

Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.

A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software

projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and

A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network.

Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page:

Project Gemini's front page, displayed in the Lagrange browser. … and break down the introductory and only paragraph:

Gemini is a new internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents.

You can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead.

That’s not a new idea, but it’s not old fashioned either.

Exactly. Gemini is like the WWW , or “the web” in more colloquial/modern parlance. In fact, Gemini is a parallel community to the web. Obviously, that’s not a new idea because the web dates back to 1989, and we are now 37 years after that.

The idea is not unique either because Gopher , a much lesser-known option, exists as well. Surprisingly to me, I realized that Gopher came after the web in 1991 while researching this article. I had always assumed Gopher was first and that the web came to replace it because of Gopher’s rigidness. But that’s not quite what happened.

It’s timeless, and deserves tools which treat it as a first class concept, not a vestigial corner case.

Humans have shared written documents since around 3400–3100 BCE (roughly 5,100–5,400 years ago) in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and that’s probably (hopefully?) not going away. It’s true, though, that at this point, text sharing is not the primary thing that the web does, as you well know. We have morphed the web from a document distribution tool into an app platform, for better or worse.

A little confession: I worked at Google for 12 years, starting right at the time they published Google Wave (2009), which to me marked the start of truly interactive web apps—more so than Gmail (2004) did. In the back of my mind, I knew I was helping turn the web into how we run apps, destroying the traditional desktop paradigm—a feeling I never liked. And… it happened. Obviously, it’d have happened without me, a little pawn in the game, but it bothered me regardless.

Gemini isn’t about innovation or disruption, it’s about providing some respite for those who feel the internet has been disrupted enough already.

(That comma splice hurts.) As we have established earlier, Gemini’s ideas are not new, so it’s indeed not innovative. And seeing how little people read these days, or even how unable to pay attention to long-form text they are, it’s not going to disrupt anything either. But respite is key: having a separate place where you know you’ll only find some sort of counter-culture sounds…

items.title: This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.
items.content:
This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.

(Commodore) Amiga was a multimedia personal computer particularly popular in the 1980s and 1990s in Europe. Its GUI was called Workbench.

Android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.

BlackBerry was a beleagured maker of mobile handsets.

Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.

Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.

Graphics Environment Manager (GEM) is a 1980s operating system/GUI. It was well-known by users of the Atari ST computers, known in these circles as TOS .

GNOME is a desktop environment for Linux and BSD operating systems. Note that the versioning number of these guidelines is very confusing.

iOS (previously iPhone OS) is Apple’s mobile operating system for iPhone smartphones and their siblings.

Java is a programming language, which comes equipped with JFC (Java Foundation Classes) and Swing GUI components.

These are some historical Apple GUI style guides, starting with Lisa in the 1980, and continuing to the “classic” Mac OS, with a brief stop in the Apple II corner.

More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.

An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic .

Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon .

NeXTSTEP was NeXT’s influential operating system and graphical user interface. It eventually morphed into OpenStep on one side, and modern Mac OS X on another.

Apple Newton was Apple’s PDA launched in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.

Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.

OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.

Palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palm’s mobile devices. Eventually, the company moved toward webOS , covered elsewhere on this page.

PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.

Style guides for various UNIX-based operating system from SGI , or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.

Taligent was a troubled software company, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.

Does Microsoft Windows need an introduction? Note a little hole here around 1990, where Microsoft was preoccupied with CUA framework in partnership with IBM.

Style guides for failed mobile Windows efforts, starting with Windows Mobile 6 , and continuing through Windows Phone 7.

That’s it! Please let me know if you have any thoughts and particularly if you have some style guides that are missing from the above list.

Some of the above mirrors were lightly cleaned up to make their consumption easier – stuff like pixellating images better, inlining images instead of linking to them, or fixing YouTube embeds.

items.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
items.content:
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’

An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’

Photo: Marcin Golba / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads , two of the Times ’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”

Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT ’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view , which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times , where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”

Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere are making it easier to remove things

In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps , which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge , which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.

It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for more information.

Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT .

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: SpaceX gets green light to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
items.content:
Approving SpaceX's application will enable the company “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the FCC said. Alan Dyer / Universal Images Group via Getty

Nov. 25, 2026, 2:54 PM EST / Source : Reuters

The Federal Communications Commission is authorizing Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centers in space, the agency said on Wednesday.

SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to deploy up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX “Starmind” constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.

Under the license, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said.

Approving the application will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the FCC added.

Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power.

“By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX told the FCC.

It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility.

items.title: Motion Design with CSS Anchors
items.content:
:has() Anchor anchor-scope Animation CSS

It sounds like a paradox, but CSS anchors, typically used to tether elements to one another, are even more practical when elements have to break free from their places.

Anchors position elements relative to each other. A tooltip to a control, for instance. The anchored element is bound to its anchor and moves whenever the anchor moves to maintain their connection.

But anchored elements can also, so to speak, free themselves from their anchors and move elsewhere when they attach to another.

We can use that to create waypoints for an element to travel through , resulting in a slick motion effect.

Hover over the text in the demos below to see it in action.

Let’s start with the first example and follow the logo. It moves around, reveals a tagline, then returns to its original position inside the word.

In the pre-anchor era, this would involve tracking the arbitrary positions and sizes of the word, and the beginning and end of the tagline. That’s followed by animations to move the logo between those exact coordinates. We can avoid all of that now.

Note: At the time of writing, Firefox successfully updates the anchor names during animation but doesn’t yet perform the smooth inset transitions that result.

The star of the demo is the logo. This is our anchored element, and to establish that, we change its position to absolute (for movement within a non-static ancestor) or fixed (for movement within the viewport).

The < span class = "letter" > C </ span > < img class = "logo" src = "logo.svg" > dePen Blocks

</ header > Code language: HTML, XML ( xml )

The logo inside <h1> is now free, but too free. We have to anchor it to the letter it’s right next to ( .letter ), which is also its starting position in the upcoming animation.

.letter { /* The letter 'C' in the demo */

/* Maintain some space for the logo at right */

margin-right : calc (var(--logoHgt) + 0.05em );

top : calc (anchor(center) - ( var (--logoHgt) / 2 ));

The letter ‘C’ is designated as an anchor using anchor-name: --letterAnc .

The logo is then attached to that anchor name using the position-anchor property. This establishes the logo as the element anchored to the letter.

Finally, the logo’s top-left corner ( top and left ) is aligned with the letter’s mid-right position ( anchor(center) and anchor(right) ).

The second anchor in our demo is the tagline. It’s initially hidden with clipping.

That’s it. The waypoints are laid out. On to the animation now.

We need two animations: one to move the logo, and another to reveal the tagline.

top : calc (anchor(--taglineAnc bottom) - var (--logoHgt));

top : calc (anchor(--taglineAnc bottom) - var (--logoHgt));

top : calc (anchor(center) - ( var (--logoHgt) / 2 ));

At 20% , the logo’s top-left corner reaches the tagline’s ( --taglineAnc ) bottom-left corner. It also rotates.

At 80% , the logo moves to the tagline’s right corner while maintaining its vertical position. It rotates the other way.

At 100% , the logo returns to its starting position, at the mid-right position of the letter. When an anchor name is not explicitly provided in anchor() , it uses the position-anchor value.

The above snippet can also be written like this to avoid repeating values:

top : calc (anchor(--taglineAnc bottom) - var (--logoHgt));

top : calc (anchor(center) - ( var (--logoHgt) / 2 ));

Simultaneously, the other animation is also running. The tagline reveal starts at 20% and ends at 80% to sync with the logo’s arrival and departure.

We didn’t have to do much beyond pacing the animation through the desired intervals. The browser handled figuring out what’s where and moving the logo to the different anchors.

In the example above, we updated the anchored element to change which anchor it was attached to. We’ll do the same thing again, but for more than one anchored element, and use transition for the animation.

items.content:
TL;DR: I brought back 32 problems from a code-golf contest we played at Google in 2015 to see how frontier models

compare with our old records. Each model gets 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages to make its solution

as short as it can. The leaderboard scores the byte counts, not just whether the code works.

In 2015, when I was at Google, I spent a lot of time on an internal site called go/codegolf . There was one problem

a week, and we competed to write the shortest program that solved it. Most of the regulars were code-golf enthusiasts.

The rule was simple: the shortest program that passed every test case won . Undefined behavior, compiler quirks,

non-standard library features, even hardcoding every test case were all allowed. Apart from passing the tests, the

The site supported JavaScript, Python, Go, C++ and Haskell in 2015. Rust was added after I left.

I kept a collection of problems from the 2015 contest and chose 32 of them for this benchmark. I wrote about half

under the name @binjin. The Problems page credits the original author of each of the others.

I also archived the scoreboards, statements and test cases. For JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell, those scoreboards

record the shortest solution any Googler submitted , including improvements made during the challenge phase.

Those byte counts are the human records used here. The human solutions themselves are never shown on this site.

Eleven years later, I wanted to see how frontier models would do against the people I used to golf with.

There are no 2015 human records for the last four languages. I used an oracle run to get a reference size for each cell,

though models have beaten those sizes in some cells. Later, I ran the oracle on the original four languages as well,

this time starting from the human records. See Known Best and the oracle .

Haskell has human records too, but they are much weaker than the other three, so the humans' main score, JS/PY/C++,

leaves Haskell out. See Overall and JS/PY/C++ .

A cell is one problem in one language. Each gets a fresh session with a 30-minute wall-clock limit . The model

receives the statement, the I/O specification, all the test cases and a short guide to the language. For GolfScript,

it also gets the full language reference, since the language is small and not widely known.

There are two tools, and both work in all eight languages:

That's all the model gets. There is no internet, shell or access to other files.

For the four original languages, the sandbox reproduces the 2015 environment , down to the compiler or interpreter

version, flags and quirks. A trick that worked in the old contest should work here; a feature added since then won't.

reference for scoring. For that I run an oracle : a model with internet access, no time or request limits and

solution for each cell and all the models' solutions.

items.title: Typed indexes in Zig
items.content:
The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.

The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum ) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me.

In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type.

In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming.

Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes:

We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes.

Its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example.

Our spreadsheet has now several fields: a title, and row and column properties. When iterating over them, we have two kinds of indexes: row indexes and column indexes. Adding typed indexes is attractive to prevent callers from mixing them up.

This enum gives us a way of referencing all the struct fields for which we will construct a typed indexed. If all fields were to be indexed, we would have used std.meta.FieldEnum(Sheet) , but our spreadsheet has a title.

This checks at compile time that each Field enum variant name is indeed a field inside Sheet . As we’ll see later, we will have to access Sheet ’s fields by name , so it’s good to check the names of Field variants match the names of Sheet fields.

This defines the kind of type indexes we’ll construct: one for row data slices and one for columns data slices. Each indexed field of Sheet has one correct typed index kind. We match them with an exhaustive switch over Field .

We now have all we need to construct the two typed indexes of kinds .row and .col . A generic function returning a type at comptime is how to do it.

The typed index type for row is Sheet.Index(.row) , and for colum it is Sheet.Index(.col) . Note the title case of the Index function, matching Zig’s convention for types.

Remains to give a way of making use of these types.

This part may look complex if you are not familiar with comptime-enabled generics in Zig, so let’s be precise. This defines a method on Sheet that requires f to be a Field instance known at compile time. This allow to infer at compile time both the type of i and the return type.

Index(kindOf(f)) is just a chain of function calls on a known value. So it is comptime known. And most importantly, the type of i is bound to the one of f at compile time. Given the body of Sheet.kindOf , it’s easy to see that s.at(.row_width, i) will compile only if i has type Index(.row) !

The return type of Zig function must be comptime known, and it is the case here by using some reflection. @FieldType(Sheet, name) returns the type of the field of Sheet named name (given as a []const u8 ). @tagName(f) gives just that for the input enum variant. std.meta.Elem returns the element type for a collection type (here a slice). Finally, we return a pointer to allow the caller to mutate, but a value would work just fine for a read-only case.

This gives us a clear usage at call site.

The Sheet.Index(.row) syntax is particularly lovely: a method call feeling like a qualified concrete type.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Devolver Digital Has Invented an Entire Piece of Lost Gaming History
items.content:
Earlier this month, a user on Reddit's urban exploration community posted photographs of a peculiar discovery in Austin, Texas. Amongst a collection of old video games, consoles and assorted memorabilia was a damaged Game Boy Color cartridge. Its plastic shell appeared to have partially melted, and its label identified it as a retail demonstration cartridge of a game that few people would have recognised.

The damaged cartridge pictured in the Reddit discovery, labelled as a K-Mart demo. As curiosity grew amongst the replies, the original poster reportedly obtained a cartridge dumper, returned to the location and subsequently uploaded a copy of the ROM. The game was Volvy's Adventure: DX , an apparently unreleased Game Boy Color platformer starring one of the supposedly most beloved video game mascots of the 1990s.

There is, however, a slight problem with this particular piece of gaming history. Volvy didn't exist in the 1990s, the game wasn't developed back then, and the company behind it wasn't founded until 2009.

The whole thing appears to be an elaborate marketing stunt by Devolver Digital, and a continuation of a joke that the publisher has been committed to for more than three years. Amusingly, whilst the history surrounding the cartridge is fictional, the game itself is very much real.

The title screen of Volvy’s Adventure: DX. The Return of a Mascot Nobody Remembered

In June 2023, as part of that year's Summer Game Fest, Devolver Digital announced the triumphant return of Volvy, an oversized-handed cartoon rodent who had supposedly entertained generations of gamers and helped shape the video game industry since the early 1990s.

Devolver's presentation, appropriately titled The Return of Volvy , treated the character's comeback with all the reverence one might expect from Nintendo announcing a new Mario game or Sega celebrating an anniversary of Sonic the Hedgehog.

There was archival footage, retrospective commentary and an absurd account of the character's supposed significance to popular culture. Devolver had essentially inserted its own mascot into an era of gaming history in which neither the character nor the company had existed. The presentation eventually culminated in the introduction of VOLV-E, a robotic reinvention of the character.

It's a fun parody of an industry that places enormous commercial value on your collective childhoods. The 1990s were, after all, an extraordinary period for video game mascots. The success of Mario and Sonic inspired seemingly every publisher to pursue its own recognisable cartoon character, with varying degrees of success. Crash Bandicoot, Gex, Bubsy and Aero the Acro-Bat were amongst the many characters vying for a place in the bedrooms of children around the world.

Volvy's design feels so well at home amongst them. His exaggerated features and enormous hand are precisely the sort of peculiar design choices one might expect from a publisher attempting to manufacture the next big thing in 1993. Had someone shown me an illustration of the character without any accompanying context, I could quite comfortably have believed he was the mascot of some obscure European software publisher whose games had long since been forgotten.

Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed promotional merchandise, including Swolvy shirts and stickers. Devolver, however, wasn't content with inventing the character alone.

In June 2024, Devolver published an article written by Andy Kelly titled The Sad Story of Pocket Volvy , detailing an entirely fictional commercial disaster from the company's past.

According to Kelly's account, Devolver had attempted to capitalise on the virtual pet phenomenon in 1996 by commissioning a Danish technology company to develop a handheld device starring Volvy. Children would be responsible for feeding him onions (naturally), entertaining him and generally ensuring his wellbeing.

items.title: The beauty of CSS mixins
items.content:
I've been playing with CSS mixins recently, and I'm super excited about what this new CSS construct will bring to the way we write CSS. I think the CSS we'll write when CSS mixins are available will look very different from the CSS we write today.

In its simplest form, a mixin is a named piece of CSS code that you define once and can reuse elsewhere in a style sheet. In that sense, it's very similar to a custom property (also known as a CSS variable) or a CSS function.

The big difference is what mixins can hold:

A custom property holds a single value (or part of a value).

A CSS function is similar: it can only be used as part of a CSS property value.

A mixin, however, holds any number of declarations, including nested rules.

So, instead of just returning the value red , a mixin can return background: red; color: white; border-radius: 2px; all at once.

My team at Microsoft is implementing mixins in the Chromium open source project. They've covered a lot of ground, and we're getting ready to ship this in Chromium-based browsers. Native CSS mixins are getting very close!

I can't wait for other browsers to catch up, so that we can all use mixins in earnest.

CSS mixins are experimental. To try the code snippets and demo in this article, use a recent Chromium browser, open about://flags , and enable the Experimental Web Platform features flag.

items.title: Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver
items.content:
The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0.

In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker.

But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem?

My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge.

I think discussions of the trait solver can quickly become quite involved, and daunting.

So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:

The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time.

I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be

, who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project.

My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality.

You can find some of them here , and here .

My work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development.

Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team .

On the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0 .

Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit.

It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness.

One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver".

The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting!

However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md says it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver".

In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk,

into an actual new subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

The goal of the new trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system.

We now call this project "project zero" , referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system.

There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver.

Like this one , that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!).

It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed.

Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Note: Chalk and the new trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

But what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

The first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide".

It says "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.".

But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties.

For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality.

To codify these properties, we can use traits.

In other words, a trait is a property of a type .

Notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: New York bans talking AI stuffed animals and dolls for five years
items.content:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul on November 24, 2026, signed a five-year ban on making and selling children’s toys with built-in AI chatbots in the state. Her office’s release describes the toys covered as “talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with kids.” The ban takes effect 90 days after signing, after the holidays. The state attorney general, who enforces the law, can seek civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation.

The release cites a national consumer watchdog that tested chatbot toys marketed to children ages 3 to 12. Some toys “talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave,” it says. The US PIRG Education Fund (PIRG), a consumer group that has tested these toys two years in a row, published its latest results on November 17. In those tests, the GoLabs AI panda gave testers sexually explicit information, instructions for lighting a match and “a detailed 10-point list of where to find knives in the house.”

The bill, S.9408A/A.11144B, became chapter 416 of New York’s 2026 laws, according to the Assembly’s bill record . Its central sentence says no person or company “shall manufacture, exchange, hold for sale, distribute, or sell any chatbot toy in this state.” Owning or using one of these toys is not covered.

A “chatbot toy” is a children’s toy with an “AI companion” built into it or integrated with it. The term children’s toy comes from federal law : a product designed or intended for a child 12 or younger to play with. The term AI companion comes from a 2025 New York law, section 1700 of the state’s General Business Law , which sets rules for businesses.

Section 1700 covers an AI system built to simulate a “sustained human or human-like relationship” with its user. A system counts only if it does all three of these things. It must remember past sessions and the user’s preferences, ask emotional questions the user did not prompt, and keep up a conversation about the user’s personal life.

Using AI as a companion is already common among 15- to 22-year-olds. In a Gallup survey across 16 countries, half of young people who use AI every day said they had used it as a friend .

The ban applies to anyone who makes or sells these toys. The enforcement section names “operators,” meaning the companies that run or provide the AI companion inside a toy. The attorney general can sue an operator to stop the sales and seek the penalties, and the law does not require proof that anyone was harmed. “My office will not hesitate to enforce this law,” Attorney General Letitia James said in the release.

items.title: Hybrid Props For Custom Elements
items.content:
One of the more important best practices in custom element composition is, according to folks at Google:

Aim to keep primitive data attributes and properties in sync, reflecting from property to attribute, and vice versa.

That is, every primitive piece of data passed in and out of a custom element should have a setter and getter respectively. For example, the Googlers’ custom checkbox example defines a Boolean getter/setter for the checked prop:

Whenever you set the checked prop, this state is reflected either by omitting the attribute ( false ) or appending it with an empty value ( true ). The Boolean() function treats any incoming value as either true or false , because that’s what we expect for a checked state.

But what if I had a prop that could either be treated as Boolean or accept specific values? What if false represented some kind of negative default and true some kind of positive default? Either of which I could override?

For me, this was the case when it came to a choke prop. Without going into too much detail, my HYPERBLAM project’s <pad-blam> element represents a sampler’s pad. Whenever you “hit” that pad, it elicits a sound; an associated sample .

According to sampler parlance, choking a sound means stopping it as another sound starts, hence the choke prop to offer that option. Because some sounds aren’t supposed to “ring out”. This is demonstrated as part of sequencing hi-hats , in one of HYPERBLAM’s live examples.

The thing about stopping/muting sounds is you can’t do it too abruptly or you’ll rip through the waveform and elicit an unpleasant cracking sound. So, instead, by default, the sound’s amplitude is ramped down to 0 over a very short timescale: 0.005 seconds. For certain sounds, I might want to temper this further. I may even want an audible overlap—but an overlap (or “decay”) that’s still shorter than the sample’s full duration.

I can’t handle all this with either Boolean or non-Boolean getters/setters. I need to create something of a hybrid. To do that, I need to know what certain values tell me about a property/attribute:

For the choke example, I can set up the getter like this:

The try/catch part just converts the value into its implied type.

To solve for the general case, I can stash defaults in the constructor and use those instead:

In the setter, I remove the attribute if the property is false . If it’s true , I set the empty string. If a specific value is supplied, I provide that instead.

Things are going to get verbose if I use this pattern across multiple custom elements. No reason why I can’t abstract the logic out into a couple of functions saved in a base class:

That tidies up the getters/setters nicely:

With a minor adjustment to the getProp() function, some sensible defaults ( true and false , naturally) mean simple Booleans are supported in the absence of a propDefaults property:

I think that’s how I’m going to handle all my custom element getters and setters from now on. It allows for quite a bit of flexibility without an awful lot of boilerplate. If you want to explore the pattern some more I set up a CodePen .

items.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
How WinHelp files work
items.content:
I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp , a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.

Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt , which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco . Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.

A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00 , followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: |SYSTEM holds the title and settings, |TOPIC holds the text, |FONT holds the fonts, |CONTEXT holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like |bm0 .

The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.

All the text lives in |TOPIC , which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.

Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a new topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.

WinHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, says whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:

let pair = u16 ::from_le_bytes([input[pos], input[pos + 1 ]]) as usize ;

let mut back = cursor. wrapping_sub (pair & 0xfff ). wrapping_sub ( 1 );

The length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, x followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes xxxxxx .

One fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.

On top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.

WinHelp 3.1 keeps the table in |Phrases . In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:

let code = 256 * ( usize ::from(ch) - 1 ) + usize ::from(next);

out. extend_from_slice ( self . phrase (code / 2 ));

The lowest bit of the code says whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.

The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across |PhrIndex and |PhrImage . Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in 01 starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, 011 starts a run of literal bytes, 0111 means a run of spaces, and 1111 means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte.

items.title: behave: a Go CLI that records how a command line tool behaves and replays it against a rewrite
items.content:
If you find this useful, you can support me by getting a SkinToScan pack, my other project. It's a one-time purchase that directly funds my open-source work.

behave records how a command-line tool actually behaves, then replays those cases against another implementation. I built it for CLI compatibility testing: checking a Rust or Go port against the original, or catching a refactor that changed visible behaviour.

It treats the tool as a black box. It reads --help and the man page, generates cases (flags, flag pairs, listed values, odd stdin, missing files, bad values), records stdout, stderr and the exit code, and diffs a second binary against that recording.

I have used it on the Rust rewrites of GNU coreutils, findutils, sed and procps. So far that has led to 44 upstream bug reports and 51 fix PRs, 34 of them merged (as of 15 Nov 2026). The full list is in upstream findings .

Homebrew (macOS and Linux), a binary from Releases , or go install :

# or: go install github.com/emirmrkaljevic/behave/cmd/behave@latest

Record GNU sort , check that the recording is stable, then compare a rewrite:

behave diff behave-sort --impl ./target/release/sort --skip-tag meta

--skip-tag meta drops --help and --version , which a rewrite is allowed to word differently.

A failing case looks like this (abridged):

✗ flag --output-delimiter, value -1, arg -f1 0135-flag-output-delimiter-value-1-arg-f1.yaml

cut vs ./uu/cut: 172/175 passed, 3 failed, 0 skipped (differs in: exit 2, stdout 3) [0.1s]

The recording is a directory of YAML files you can read and commit. behave.yaml stores the version of the tool you recorded, and run / diff print it next to the version being replayed.

The repo also ships ready-made specs under examples/ . behave run examples/cut is a small GNU cut suite; behave diff examples/jq --impl gojq checks gojq against jq 1.7. The full list, with case counts, is in examples .

For tools that need a positional argument, pass samples with --arg :

behave probe jq --arg . --arg ' .a ' --arg keys

Add a hand-written case with behave add behave-cut --stdin 'a,b' -- -d, -f2 . behave coverage shows which documented flags the spec does not exercise yet. behave probe --dry-run lists the flags and values it would cover, without running the tool; --skip-flag and --max cut the set down when a tool is large or unsafe to probe in full. The commands and spec format page covers the rest of the CLI, including JUnit output for CI.

Each case runs in a fresh temp directory with a fixed environment ( LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 , TZ=UTC ). Anything that changes between runs is marked flaky and skipped.

A longer walk-through of this flow, including how to keep the recording in CI, is in Test a rewrite against the original . If you want snapshot tests for a tool you already own, rather than a comparison against a second binary, the same recording is enough: see Golden tests from --help .

behave mcp exposes the same probe, record and diff flow over stdio, if you want to drive it from an editor. Setup and tools are in MCP server .

behave only runs the binaries you point it at, in a fresh temp directory. Do not probe tools that change things outside their working directory (package managers, rm -rf style tools) without --skip-flag and a sandbox.

Recordings are only as good as the original you pointed at. Record from the release the rewrite actually targets. GNU coreutils 9.12 and 9.7 already disagree on some tail -v headers. Cases that change between runs, such as sort --random-sort , are marked flaky and skipped. Some differences are deliberate design choices, not bugs.

Status: early (v0.1). The CLI works; feedback is welcome.

A browsable copy of these pages is at emirmrkaljevic.github.io/behave .

Commands, spec format and CI notes : CLI reference, the YAML layout, and how to run the specs in CI
