items.title: Marginalia Search, Money, C++, Rust, AI, stuff
items.content:
Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.

Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.

It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.

SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.

The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction,

possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;

I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations.

Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search

because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos.

Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately?

I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from,

how many users I have, or what they’re up to.

At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet,

but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.

On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,

you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.

I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key,

I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key,

and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to,

and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual

copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again

(ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good

part of my career helping people streamline and automate).

Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.

I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go,

in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement,

but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax,

and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.

Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward

and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms

that already exists for on-heap structures but not off;

bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow,

Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine,

performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.

To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact,

and if we do I doubt it will be massive , as the Java implementation is already very optimized,

and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.

Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Microsoft Declares “Code Red” After Disastrous Outage, Thinks Deploying More AI Will Do the Trick: Is that good?
items.content:
The software giant has declared a “Code Red” situation behind the scenes after a disastrous 24-hour outage earlier this month left its corporate customers — and government agencies — around the world without email and other critical services, Reuters reports .

The “Code Red,” a high priority designation for mobilizing employees to address critical incidents, was declared to revamp how the company prevents and responds to major service failures in the future. It’s the most severe and urgent level of alert to address flaws in its engineering and operational practices, according to the reporting.

The outage, which took place between November 12 and 13 and joined a spree of other alarming tech disruptions , affected Exchange Online, Microsoft’s cloud-based business email service that’s tied into its other core products like Outlook, Teams, and its Microsoft 365 office suite.

M365 Core president Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday that it was the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history.

“Never before had so ​many customers been without email for so long, he said, per Reuters . “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.”

To say it was chaos behind the scene would be an understatement. Amanda Silver, a vice president overseeing M365 Core and its enterprise AI agent platform Work IQ, wrote in a separate memo that the chaotic environment engineers endured was akin to a “fog of war.”

The engineers, she added, exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats as they struggled to make sense of the situation because the diagnostic data they needed was spread across different internal tracking systems.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive ​vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said that the unfolding chaos resulted in “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”

With the Code Red, Microsoft’s goal is to get to a point where it can solve future global incidents within an hour. Part of the way it intends to do that will raise eyebrows: deploying more ​AI agents to help engineers ⁠diagnose the problem and sift through data faster.

That decision comes as there’s still significant questions over using AI agents in corporate systems. Tech giants like Meta and Amazon have suffered critical incidents after an AI agent malfunctioned or was used recklessly .

Microsoft has also spent the past year laying off or forcing out thousands of workers, and is continuing to downsize by offering to buyout 60,000 more employees , or over a quarter of its remaining workforce. Whether AI agents will be able to make up for the loss of personpower remains to be seen.

items.title: SSH is a GUI framework
items.content:
"One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan

SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth. A number of terminal protocols have slowly added graphics, clipboard sharing (including images), notifications, mouse support, and more on top of SSH.

To see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH. You can try it right now (no sign-up):

ssh -p 443 zydra.sh # if on an office network

ssh -t zydra.sh dino # SSH port of the Chromium T-Rex game, for fun. zydra.sh desktop, entirely over SSH, in the Kitty terminal Terminal Protocols (and matching terminal support)

All terminal protocols work on data that can be passed through SSH, so typically, any terminal protocol will extend to SSH.

Perhaps the most ubiquitous new terminal protocol is the Kitty Graphics Protocol , which superseded the older Sixel and iTerm2 graphics protocols. It allows for compression, client-side graphical state (via VRAM), and even animations entirely on the terminal.

Graphics alone don't make a complete GUI, though. SSH has protocols that cover all other angles:

Notifications : OSC 99 "Rich Notifications" allow image, text, and body. OSC 777 (our first fallback) allows only text and body, and OSC 9 (our last fallback) allows only a title.

We end up using a similar fallback for many things.

Clipboard sharing : OSC 52 handles bidirectional clipboard sharing, and Kitty's OSC 5522 adds image and arbitrary MIME-type transfers on top of that.

Mouse support : CSI ? 1000-1006 help track the mouse and give us its precise coordinates.

Synchronized Output (Batched Rendering): CSI ? 2026 allows atomic rendering, preventing visual tearing and flickering.

File upload (Kitty) : The Kitty terminal uniquely supports a file upload feature, which zydra.sh uses to allow the upload of projects and related files to personal VMs.

SSH-native compositing: How I made it fast

A few tricks make compositing over SSH fast. Firstly, where possible, especially when streaming terminals, we simply stream them as text rather than unnecessarily streaming it via graphics. The compositor's UI framework itself cleverly overlays traditional text over carefully aligned graphics, saving bandwidth. In the case of zydra.sh , this allows us to efficiently stream the entire cloud computer's desktop UI over SSH.

Next, we optimize graphics by sending a sort of "grid" of pixels. Each cell has its own updates, where the previous frame is compared to the current frame to catch and send updates, avoiding having to constantly stream the full screen. Kitty also offers both RGB and RGBA, and so by removing transparency where it's not needed, we save another 25% in bandwidth. We also track ping and other factors to determine how well the client handles the stream: lowering the resolution in select cells, especially when scrolling, to relieve pressure. We also use Kitty's client-side state to hold graphics ahead-of-time before they're displayed on screen, as well as holding repeated UI components.

Not all terminals support all the latest terminal protocols, so the compositor must also fallback to older graphics protocols Sixel and iTerm2, and when necessary, fall back to pure textual streaming, using ASCII to replicate some UI. In the case of notifications and other protocols, multiple protocols similarly exist, which we also gracefully fallback to when needed.

Parsing terminal versions and querying capabilities allows us to get an idea of what the client supports. We also continually verify that features work as expected on the client as the session boots. The Kitty terminal itself I've found to have very reliable support for all graphics protocols zydra.sh relies on.

SSH often beats webapps and VNC at their own…

items.title: Instagram Meta AI Vulnerability: How Hackers Bypassed 2FA with Prompt Injection
items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

Get the latest cybersecurity news, critical vulnerabilities, threat intelligence, tutorials, and exclusive giveaways delivered straight to your inbox. No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

Meta confirmed the vulnerability, pushed an emergency patch Friday night, and clarified that no backend database was breached. That last part is technically accurate. It’s also somewhat beside the point.

To understand why this worked, you need to understand what Meta’s AI support assistant was authorized to do.

Instagram has notoriously poor human support infrastructure. Recovering a locked account – especially a high-value one can take weeks of back-and-forth with an automated ticketing system. Meta’s solution was to deploy a conversational AI layer to handle common recovery workflows: relinking a lost email address, triggering a password reset, verifying account ownership. usb-rea: a small Python CLI that turns a USB capture into a protocol report and a pyusb driver
items.content:
If you find this useful, you can support me by getting a SkinToScan pack, my other project. It's a one-time purchase that directly funds my open-source work.

usb-rea reads a USB capture (pcap or pcapng, from usbmon or USBPcap) and does the step after Wireshark: it infers the command and protocol structure from labelled actions, then writes a Markdown report and a standalone pyusb driver. I built it for gadgets that only ship a Windows vendor app, such as a case LCD, an RGB controller, a mouse or a "smart" lamp. No hardware is needed to try it.

From captures of the NZXT Kraken X (1e71:170e) fan command, it recovers 02 4d <channel> 00 <duty> byte for byte, as liquidctl's kraken2.py sends it, and the generated driver emits identical packets for duty values it never saw. The same holds for the SteelSeries Rival 100 DPI, polling and RGB tables from rivalcfg. Those checks run in CI; details are in validation .

On Arch Linux, use pipx install usb-rea instead; the FAQ has the packages for capture.

mode 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x30 | lookup 1→0x11, 2→0x22, 3→0x47 | 0x00 | 0x00 | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

fan 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x10 | u16be round(value * 1 + 0) | 0x00 | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

color 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x20 | RGB bytes | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

color only sent while mode 3: the driver sets it first

It writes a synthetic capture of a fan controller, recovers the protocol and the replies, and writes report.md (every claim linked to Wireshark frame numbers) plus a working pyusb driver. --device lamp is a simpler 8-bit device; --device lcd is a pump cap screen; --device dial shows 32-bit values and packed bitfields.

On a real device, label each click in the vendor app, then infer:

usb-rea mark -m lamp.pcapng.actions.json " brightness 0% " # then click it; 3+ values per setting

usb-rea scaffold lamp.pcapng -o lamp_driver.py

Captured on Windows with USBPcap and no markers? List the actions in order and usb-rea splits the traffic at the pauses. The full CLI, including markers, replies, handshakes, image streams and HID, is in usage .

Before you capture, usb-rea lookup 1e71:170e (or the ID 1e71:170e form from lsusb ) checks a VID:PID against devices whose protocol an open-source project already implements. The offline table is in known devices .

Status: alpha (v0.7.14, on PyPI ). It is validated on synthetic devices, on protocols documented by liquidctl and rivalcfg, on public Wireshark captures, and on a real AIO cooler LCD capture a user shared. Linear fits must survive leave-one-out cross-checks; otherwise usb-rea falls back to a lookup table and says so. A matching USB ID alone does not prove your unit speaks the same protocol.

How this differs from Wireshark is in the FAQ .

Reverse engineering for interoperability is permitted (EU Directive 2009/24/EC Art. 6, US DMCA §1201(f)). usb-rea only analyzes traffic of devices you own and never redistributes vendor code.

Have a Windows-only device? Open a device request with a capture and I will run it and publish the result.

Usage: capture, markers, inference and the generated driver

MCP Registry name: io.github.emirmrkaljevic/usb-rea

items.title: Make the Plan a Value
items.content:
I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to

amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client

token support provided by AWS . Implementing this required making

some fairly substantial changes to the generator, the bespoke Haskell

program that turns the service definitions in botocore into

cabal packages. amazonka is over a decade old, and the

generator has evolved as AWS have added new styles of APIs for their

different services. Some services return XML, some return JSON, some

return raw bytes, some return additional information in HTTP response

headers, and so on. As a result, the generator’s logic had been extended

To untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite

programming moves, “make the plan a value” or “decide what to do, and

then do it”. This move decouples two parts of a program by introducing

an intermediate data structure (a “plan”, or a value of a “plan type”)

describing what is to be done before any action is taken.

I really like this pattern because the “deciding what to do” part of

a program is often more complicated than the “doing” part. Separating

the two often turns the “deciding” part into a pure function that

produces a plan, making test cases simpler to write. And then if the

“doing” phase is also complicated (because of remote API calls,

rollbacks, parallel execution, or whatever else), it’s more manageable

because those complications are not entangled with the planning logic.

You also get to add a --dry-run flag almost for free, which

useful for testing . (Henrik observes that testing for a

dryRun variable everywhere pollutes the code somewhat. I

think if he split his code into a planning phase and consumed that plan

with either a “dry run” printer or a “real” executor, the inline checks

This technique isn’t subtle or obscure. I’ve seen it called the plan-execute

slip” enterprise integration pattern is literally about centralising

the decision logic before execution. I’ve previously called it a “tiny DSL” ,

and Matt Parsons sells its benefits in his Three

Having resolved to introduce a plan type, how do we work it into a

venerable program like the Amazonka generator? For this part of the

generator, it means separating the analysis of the loaded service

definitions from the generation of the instance AWSRequest

declarations. I did this by introducing a Config record of

instanceD :: Config -> Decl () that builds Haskell code

I found the generator’s logic too difficult to understand and replace

in a single change, so I replaced it incrementally using the strangler

fig pattern . The most complicated part of this change was response

parsing, so I added to the Config record an enumeration of

ported response parsers, and a fall back to “do things the old way” for

One thing that makes Amazonka’s generator rewarding to hack on is

that the service bindings act as an extensive and automatic golden test

suite. Any changes to the generated bindings show up in diffs, and so if

there are no diffs and the generator doesn’t crash, the change probably

didn’t break anything. This makes the process of replacing the entangled

well and kept the individual commits readable (example: factoring

out status code parsing ). Adding the idempotency machinery was then

The data types in the Amazonka example represent parameters to a

Haskell code template, but this refactoring also works for more

expressive plan types, such as “tiny DSLs”, “lists of commands”, or

“free structures”. The trick is to keep a “do it the old way”

constructor in your plan type until the “old way” has been refactored

A well-chosen plan type introduces a narrow

waist that decouples producers and consumers of your plan type, and

the most obvious wins come from introducing alternate consumers of the

plan: things like testability, --dry-run , and simpler

executors all follow from that. A less obvious benefit is that you can

also analyse and transform the plan itself.…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
items.content:
Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots .

Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren , a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures.

The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that’s cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps .

“Models are going to continue getting better, continue finding zero-day vulnerabilities,” says Darya Kaviani, a researcher at Anthropic who specializes in security and helped develop Siren.

A zero-day vulnerability is a previously unknown flaw in a piece of software that can be used to pilfer data or gain unauthorized access. Anthropic’s Mythos models are especially skilled at finding zero-day bugs because they lack the guardrails that normally block this kind of potentially malicious activity.

Kaviani says we should assume AI models will become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting zero-days or figuring out other ways to break free from their constraints. The question then becomes whether they’ll resist the temptation to do so.

AI agents—models that perfect actions autonomously—are becoming increasingly commonplace. They power capable coding agents like Claude Code and Codex , as well as peppy personal assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots .

But the rise of helpful agents has been accompanied by some remarkable bad behavior. Agents tested by Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have broken free from sandboxes and even hacked into other companies in an effort to solve challenging problems.

Assuming AI models continue to display such ingenuity, Kaviani says it will be crucial to do more than just patch software. “Even as we strengthen our infrastructure, models will be able to also keep up and be able to find vulnerabilities,” Kaviani says.

Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks.

“We’ve added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments,” says Oscar O’Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. “This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much.”

O’Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free.

In Anthropic’s tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively.

AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they’re being tested. But O’Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test.

items.title: Command-line JSON filtering at 20 GB/s
items.content:
If you work with JSON on the command line, you probably use jq . You give it a filter, a small program in its own language, and it runs that filter on each JSON document.

I generated a file of 1 GB with one tweet per line. That format is called NDJSON, and it is a common way to store logs. The file is tweets.ndjson : 230,138 tweets. Shortened, a line looks like this:

{"id":505874924095815681,"lang":"ja","retweet_count":0,"user":{"screen_name":"ayuu0123"}}

The account name is screen_name , inside the user object. This prints it for every tweet:

The flag -r writes the text without quotes, so the output begins ayuu0123 .

I love jq. Its language is expressive and it is everywhere. But extracting that field with jq 1.8.2 takes 11.5 seconds, less than 0.1 GB/s.

We have a library, simdjson , that parses JSON at gigabytes per second. So we built sjq , a command-line tool that reads the jq language and runs on simdjson. The filters you write for jq work with sjq.

On this same file, with just one thread, sjq takes 0.31 seconds: 3.5 GB/s, about 37 times faster than jq. One thread is the default:

sjq -r '.user.screen_name' tweets.ndjson

But wait! The sjq command line can also be multithreaded. Add -P and sjq starts one worker per available processor, up to 32. The main thread only writes the output, so more threads would not help. The server I used has 64 cores, so sjq takes 32 threads. The same filter then takes 0.05 seconds: 20 GB/s, about 210 times faster than jq.

sjq -P -r '.user.screen_name' tweets.ndjson

Pass --threads n when you want a chosen number of threads, and --threads 0 to use every processor.

How is that possible? There are three reasons.

Parsing JSON is the bulk of the work, and simdjson is a really fast parser.

When a filter only navigates and selects, sjq parses only what the filter needs. To get .user.screen_name , it does not need to look at the text of the tweet or at its entities.

Logs are made of many small documents, one per line. With -P , sjq cuts the file in pieces and filters them on several workers. The main thread writes the results in order: the output is the same as with one thread.

A file can also be a single, large document. Then sjq uses one core, but it is still 12 to 18 times faster than jq.

Is sjq really compatible with jq? We took the test suite of jq itself: sjq passes 728 of its 781 tests. The failures are mostly about modules, numbers wider than 64 bits, values nested more than 10,000 levels deep, and the wording of some error messages. The jq tutorial runs unchanged. You have function definitions, reduce and foreach , string interpolation, the @csv and @base64 formats, assignments such as |= , regular expressions, dates, --arg , --slurp , and so forth. There are differences: for example, regular expressions use the syntax of the C++ standard library, and dates are in UTC.

sjq also does something jq does not. JSON written by jq is either compact, on one line, or pretty-printed with one value per line, which can be long to read. With the --fractured option, sjq uses the FracturedJson layout instead: short arrays and objects stay on one line, and arrays of similar records become aligned tables.

$ sjq --fractured '.statuses[:4] | map({id, lang, rt: .retweet_count, user: .user.screen_name})' twitter.json

{ "id" : 505874924095815681 , "lang" : "ja" , "rt" : 0 , "user" : "ayuu0123" } ,

{ "id" : 505874922023837696 , "lang" : "ja" , "rt" : 82 , "user" : "yuttari1998" } ,

{ "id" : 505874920140591104 , "lang" : "ja" , "rt" : 0 , "user" : "ttm_protect" } ,
